item.title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5 Is Now Less in Your Face, Less Performance-Hogging
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Nvidia has updated its DLSS 5 technology, aiming to make it less intrusive and more performance-efficient. The company has been promoting AI-driven graphics as the future of gaming, but earlier versions of DLSS 5 faced criticism for altering in-game visuals in ways that deviated from developers’ artistic intent. Notable examples included distorted character appearances in games like *Resident Evil Requiem* and *Hogwarts Legacy*, where AI-generated lighting and textures led to unrealistic changes, such as aging characters or exaggerated lighting effects. In response, Nvidia claims its latest updates allow developers to preserve their original artistic vision while enhancing realism through lifelike lighting and materials. New screenshots show less drastic visual changes, with DLSS 5 now available in *Hogwarts Legacy* and *Where Winds Meet*. The AI now focuses on subtle improvements, such as brighter scenery and refined details without drastically altering textures or adding unnecessary facial features. Nvidia also highlights performance gains, reducing DLSS 5’s GPU VRAM usage by 20% and shrinking its parameter count to 118 million. This improvement means frame rate drops are less severe, potentially benefiting older games through modding tools like RTX Remix. Nvidia’s new RTX Spark PCs, including the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, are designed to run DLSS 5, though performance still requires upscaling and frame generation for playable framerates. The company acknowledges that the trade-off between enhanced visuals and performance remains a user choice. The article notes that Nvidia’s updates aim to address past criticisms while balancing technical efficiency with artistic fidelity. (Full disclosure: travel and lodging were paid by Nvidia, and Gizmodo did not guarantee coverage as a condition of accepting the trip).

item.title: iClever Q950 Review: Kid-Friendly Headphones That Protect Young Ears
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The iClever Q950 headphones ($69.99) are a redesigned version of the earlier iClever BTH20, which earned an Editors’ Choice award for kids’ headphones. The Q950 retains key features like AAC support, active noise cancellation (ANC), ambient pass-through mode, and an 80dBA volume limiter to protect children’s hearing. It features a more mature design compared to the BTH20, including a hard-shell case instead of a bag, and is priced slightly higher at $69. While not surpassing the BTH20’s acclaim, the Q950 offers a high-quality alternative for pre-teens who prefer its updated look. The headphones come in blue or purple, with a mix of plastics that feel smooth but may appear somewhat cheap. The headband is stretchy and adjustable, with reinforced folding yokes for compact storage. The included semi-rigid carrying case has a mesh pocket for cables. Comfort is notable, with thick, plush foam cushions and a weight of 8.9 ounces, though the firm clamping force may bother some children. Internally, 40mm drivers and SafeSound 2.0 technology limit audio output to 80dBA, while SafeSound 3.0 adds ANC, earning TÜV Rheinland Hearing Care Certification for safe audio levels. Controls are on the right earcup, including volume, power, play/pause, and ANC settings. The headphones support ANC and pass-through but lack LE Audio, Auracast, and Bluetooth Multipoint. A unique audio sharing feature allows two pairs to sync via triple-tapping power buttons. Only AAC and SBC codecs are supported. Battery life is rated at 60 hours with ANC off and 35 hours with ANC on, with a user-replaceable battery. Charging via USB-A to C is included, though no charger comes in the box. The wear sensor pauses playback when removed and turns off after five minutes of inactivity. ANC provides decent noise reduction for kids, muffling low-frequency sounds but not fully eliminating high-frequency ambient noise. Transparency mode offers subtle environmental awareness. Audio quality emphasizes bass, with clear midrange but lacking brightness in high frequencies due to SafeSound’s 3-6kHz attenuation. While not ideal for audiophiles or complex music, the Q950 delivers a casual listening experience with minimal latency for videos. The microphones are mentioned but the review cuts off, leaving their performance unspecified. Overall, the Q950 balances safety, comfort, and functionality for children, though its price and design may not appeal to all.

item.title: Sony Bravia Theater Trio Review: A 3-Piece Spatial Audio Orchestra
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Sony's Bravia Theater Trio ($2,199.99) is a three-speaker system designed to balance simplicity with immersive spatial audio, offering a middle ground between a single soundbar and a multi-speaker setup. The system includes a center speaker (2.4 x 23 x 6.4 inches) and two side satellites (13.2 x 6.2 x 6.4 inches), which wirelessly pair with the center unit. It produces a calibrated spatial audio field larger and more precise than soundbars like the Sonos Arc Ultra ($1,099), though it lacks rear surrounds and a subwoofer, which can be added at extra cost. The Samsung HW-Q990H ($1,999.99) is noted as a more affordable Editors’ Choice alternative for spatial audio. The center speaker connects via HDMI eARC, HDMI input, USB, and power, while satellites only have power ports. All components can be mounted on walls or placed on surfaces. The system supports Dolby Atmos, DTS:X, and high-res audio formats via HDMI, with Bluetooth 6.0 for LDAC and AAC codecs. However, it lacks Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. Setup requires the Bravia Connect app and an audio probe (USB-C microphone) to calibrate the system to the user’s seating position. The app also manages volume, bass, modes, and source selection. Without rear surrounds or a subwoofer, the trio delivers strong front soundstage and directional imaging, as heard in scenes from *Raiders of the Lost Ark* and *Avatar: The Legend of Aang*, though low-frequency rumble and rear effects are absent. The system’s volume control lacks a numerical display on the TV, relying on a simple icon. Physical controls are absent, requiring the remote or app for adjustments. Optional upgrades include rear surround speakers (Theater Rear 8 or 9) and subwoofers (Theater Sub 7, 8, or 9). While the trio excels in spatial audio for movies and music, its high price and reliance on optional components may deter some buyers.

item.title: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Amazon's premium tablet gets almost everything right
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Amazon's latest premium tablet, is positioned as a strong competitor to Apple's iPad Air and Pro. Unlike previous Fire tablets, which focused on basic media consumption, the 12 Pro runs full Android with access to the Google Play Store and Amazon's own apps. It features a 12-inch display with a 3:2 aspect ratio, 2,800 x 1,840 resolution (280 pixels per inch), and a 120Hz refresh rate, making it one of the most advanced displays in its price range. The screen includes an optional $50 nanomatte finish that significantly reduces glare, though colors may appear washed out under strong light. The tablet's design mirrors Apple's iPad with a thin aluminum unibody, 6.5mm thickness, and 1.21-pound weight, slightly thicker and heavier than the 11-inch iPad Air. It includes a USB-C port, a four-pin keyboard connector, and a magnetic pen slot. The device emphasizes Amazon services like Kindle, Prime Video, and Audible on the home screen but also supports Google apps and third-party downloads. While the software isn't as optimized as iPadOS, the combination of a high-refresh-rate display, anti-reflective finish, and Amazon's ecosystem makes it a compelling value at $499. The tablet excels as a reading device, with the Kindle app offering dark mode, blue light reduction, and customizable display profiles for extended use. Despite minor software limitations, its affordability and feature set position it as a strong alternative to Apple's premium tablets.

item.title: Global phone shipments plummet—research marks largest drop in over a decade
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central
Global smartphone shipments reached their lowest level in 14 years during Q3 2026, according to Counterpoint Research, marking a 20% year-over-year decline. The market downturn is attributed to extreme memory shortages driven by AI demand, which have pushed the industry into a more selective phase. Samsung retained the top position with a 3% YoY decline in shipments but saw its market share grow by 23%—the largest gain among major manufacturers—thanks to strong sales of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra, as well as the Galaxy A series. Apple followed closely behind, but its iPhone 18 lineup, which lacks a base model and only offers Pro and Pro Max variants, contributed to its decline. Chinese manufacturers Xiaomi, OPPO, and Vivo also faced significant drops in shipments. Counterpoint senior analyst Shilpi Jain noted that consumer behavior has shifted, with users holding onto devices longer, prioritizing refurbished options, and favoring higher-value phones. Omdia’s Q2 data showed a 4% YoY decline, but Samsung and Apple saw growth compared to other OEMs, though both firms warned of continued challenges in Q3 and Q4. The memory crisis, combined with elevated component costs and weaker affordability, has led OEMs to prioritize profitability over volume. Samsung is reportedly cutting Q4 production by 20-30% as a result. Analysts predict recovery is unlikely until component costs and supply conditions improve, with the budget phone market also facing uncertainty. The trend reflects broader economic pressures, as consumers increasingly weigh the cost of new devices against the value of existing ones.

item.title: 6 Obsidian plugins that convinced me to delete my other productivity tools
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
The author conducted a self-audit of their digital tools, eliminating apps and media they no longer used frequently. This process led them to replace several productivity apps with Obsidian plugins, which they found more integrated and efficient. Key plugins include Importer, Wikipedia Helper, Excalidraw, Tasks, Kanban, and QuickAdd. Importer streamlines note transfers into Obsidian, while Wikipedia Helper provides seamless access to Wikipedia content within the app, though not fully replacing browser searches. Excalidraw, a visual thinking tool, has largely replaced draw.io for creating flowcharts and diagrams, used for both website design and music project planning. Tasks, a to-do list plugin, replaced Todoist by allowing task management within Obsidian, with features like due dates and reminders. Kanban, a community plugin, serves as a Kanban board for organizing projects like a YouTube channel, mimicking past Tasker app functionality. QuickAdd enables rapid note creation via templates and shortcuts, enhancing workflow efficiency. The author appreciates Obsidian’s role as a centralized tool, reducing reliance on third-party apps while retaining specialized tools for specific tasks. They highlight the convenience of storing notes in markdown for easy export and the flexibility of combining plugins to create a customizable productivity system. The author remains excited about expanding their 'second brain' with Obsidian, emphasizing its adaptability for complex workflows and creative projects.

item.title: CMF's speakers are colorful cartons of fun—you can even 3D print your own designs

CMF has launched its first speakers, the Speaker S and Speaker M, designed to resemble classic milk cartons. item.title: ‘Street Fighter’ Is Exactly What You Hoped and Feared It Would Be
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Director Kitao Sakurai’s *Street Fighter* opens with a 1987 animated sequence depicting Ryu (Andrew Koji) winning the first World Warrior Tournament, only for his master Gouken (Don Lee) to be murdered shortly after. By 1993, Ryu has vanished from public life, cutting off contact with Ken (Noah Centineo), his former training partner. Meanwhile, Ken has become a celebrity, appearing in stunt fights with exotic animals, but feels unfulfilled. When Chun-Li (Callina Liang) invites him to the second World Warrior Tournament hosted by M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), Ken sees it as a chance to regain respect. Ryu, initially reluctant, also joins the tournament. The film’s first half is praised for its stylish, campy tone, respectful nods to the source material, and well-choreographed fight scenes. Titmouse’s 2D animation sequences effectively separate past and present timelines, adding visual flair. However, the plot unravels during the second tournament, devolving into disjointed subplots and confusing transitions. A 10-minute sequence serves no narrative purpose, while scenes lack cohesion and feel rushed. Editing choices, such as presenting a sequence out of order, further muddle the narrative. The film’s focus on setting up a sequel leaves major conflicts unresolved, and its themes remain underdeveloped. While the creative team clearly admires Capcom’s games, the movie’s incoherent storytelling and shoddy editing undermine its potential as a fun action film. Despite its flaws, *Street Fighter* retains charm through Easter eggs and a tone that leans into its campy, self-aware style. The film, which opens on October 16, struggles to balance spectacle with narrative, ultimately distracting from its action sequences with poor pacing and unresolved arcs.

item.title: I Got Lost in the Surreal Fantasia of ‘A Garden of Spheres’ and Loved Every Moment of It
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
A Garden of Spheres, a graphic novel by Swedish illustrator and comic book author Linnea Sterte, presents a surreal, expansive fantasy world that defies conventional storytelling. The series follows an immortal demigod of destruction with no memory of her identity, wandering a vast, ever-shifting landscape to uncover her purpose. Unlike traditional fantasy narratives, the story unfolds as a series of vignettes, shifting focus among characters and across time, with its mythos expanding organically as it progresses. Sterte’s world is populated by dragons born from spheres in riverbeds, each hatching to create new biomes of flora and fauna. Some dragons are tamed, others hunted or revered as gods, while the world itself is shaped by a pantheon of deities who create life and monsters based on their whims. The un-maker, the central figure, exists outside the rules of gods and dragons, possessing only the power to destroy. Her journey through this alien world is marked by encounters with diverse civilizations, rulers, and ethereal beings, all while navigating a geography where time dilates with distance from a central water-enclosed region. The first volume’s art style, characterized by lavish, water-painted panels and minimal dialogue, immerses readers in a visually arresting experience that prioritizes atmosphere over plot. While the dense world-building and naming conventions initially posed challenges, an appendix in Peow’s edition clarifies key revelations, such as the world’s likely flat geography and time dilation effects. The author praises the anthology-style detours, including stories like two rival warriors exchanging god-lore or a queer woman’s political entanglements in an arranged marriage, which highlight the series’ depth and unpredictability. Sterte’s approach—crafting the world in real time as the unnamed protagonist explores it—transforms what might be seen as aimless fantasy into a strength, allowing readers to be surprised by the unbridled weirdness of its storytelling. The reviewer recommends the series as a fresh, immersive experience for fans of surreal fantasy, emphasizing its unique blend of myth-making, artistry, and open-ended exploration.

item.title: Inde Navarrette on Where Her ‘Obsession’ Character Could Go Next
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Inde Navarrette, known for her role as Nikki in the film *Obsession*, has become a prominent figure in Hollywood following her performance. She is set to host the Saturday Night Live Halloween episode and will star as Rogue in Marvel’s upcoming X-Men movie, scheduled for release in May 2028. Navarrette is also positioned as a strong contender for best actress awards as the industry gears up for its awards season. She expressed openness to continuing Nikki’s story if a sequel to *Obsession* is greenlit, discussing the character’s post-movie struggles during an interview with the Hollywood Reporter’s Awards Chatter podcast. Navarrette highlighted Nikki’s unresolved legal issues and emotional turmoil after the film’s events, noting that the character’s journey is far from over. She described Nikki’s state as beginning a grief process, emphasizing the difficulty of coping with loss of autonomy and traumatic experiences. 'She’s just starting the grief process,' Navarrette said, stressing the importance of addressing the non-pretty realities of Nikki’s situation rather than glossing over them. Beyond *Obsession*, Navarrette reflected on her career trajectory, acknowledging the high demand for her talent while advocating for careful decision-making. She emphasized her desire to focus on grounded, thoughtfully developed characters, stating, 'I really want to be specific with the next couple of my decisions to really solidify what I want to do in this industry.' Navarrette’s comments underscore her commitment to both her craft and the authenticity of her roles, balancing her rising fame with a measured approach to her future projects.

item.title: GuliKit TT Max review: The granddaddy of Switch 2 controllers
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The GuliKit TT Max is positioned as the largest and heaviest Switch 2 controller, designed for users with larger hands and offering a multiplatform gaming experience. Wider, thicker, and heavier than Nintendo’s Pro Controller or 8BitDo’s Ultimate 2, the TT Max features aligned TMR thumbsticks, four removable back paddles, a customizable floating D-pad, and multiplatform support for PC, Android, iOS, Switch, and Switch 2. Its design mimics Xbox-style controllers while incorporating PlayStation-like precision with DualSense-style aligned joysticks. The metal rear paddles, raised above the grips, add a tactile click and contribute to the controller’s substantial feel. Triggers are textured with a switch between smooth Hall effect and digital click modes, while the matte plastic face and heavily textured rear grips enhance grip. The floating D-pad supports 4-way or 8-way modes, and the included stick kit provides additional height options with silicone caps. The controller’s RGB lighting system includes four modes—constant on, stick tracing, trigger tracing, and rainbow—and serves as a visual indicator for thumbstick sensitivity settings (pink for 50%, blue for 100%, green for 150%). Haptic feedback options include gyro controls and three modes: rotary motor, maglev haptics, and HD vibration. HD vibration, the default for Switch 2, offers precise rumble but produces a grinding noise, while maglev is quieter and preferred. The controller can wake up the Switch 2 with a home button press and charges via USB-C, lasting up to 26 hours with RGB off or 14 hours with lights on low. Accessories include three analog stick pairs, four metal paddles, and a user manual. Priced at $70, the TT Max is $20 cheaper than the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller. The article highlights its versatility for AAA games like Elden Ring, Cyberpunk 2077, and Resident Evil Requiem, as well as cross-platform compatibility, making it a robust option for Switch 2 users seeking a premium, customizable controller.

item.title: Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: a full-featured robovac let down by subpar performance
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete is a flagship robot vacuum with high suction (up to 42,000Pa), an extendable side brush (12cm reach) and mop arm (17cm reach), a bagless dust tank, and quiet operation. Despite these features, its performance falls short of expectations. During testing, it failed to pick up oats, tea, and chia seeds from a mid-pile carpet even after two passes on its Max suction setting, requiring a Dyson V15 Detect for cleanup. The side brush does not remain extended along room edges, retracting inconsistently and missing dirt in corners. The mop arm, while better than the side brush, also retracts prematurely, leaving some areas uncleaned. Dual rotating mop pads performed poorly compared to rollers, worsening spills like soy sauce and requiring high water flow for damp floors. Docking issues were frequent, with the robot needing manual intervention or multiple attempts to return to the base for charging. The companion app, similar to Dreame’s, was slow on iOS and had hidden settings. Priced at $1,299 / £1,219 / AU$3,299, it competes with models like the Roborock Saros 20 Flow and Dreame Aqua20 Ultra Roller, but its performance shortcomings make it a hard sell at this price. While it includes replacement brushes, mop pads, and a dust tank to reduce ongoing costs, the review recommends cheaper alternatives like the Roborock Saros 10 or Dreame Aqua10 Ultra for better value. The Mova V70 Ultra Complete’s high price and mixed feature performance fail to deliver a cohesive package, leaving it underwhelming despite its advanced specs.

item.title: Withings wants new users to pay $100 a year to sync with Apple Health
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Withings has implemented a new policy requiring new users to pay $100 annually to sync health data with Apple Health or other third-party apps, sparking backlash from existing customers. The change, effective October 13, gates automatic data synchronization to its subscription service, Withings+. Current users are unaffected, but accounts created after the cutoff date must subscribe to Withings+ to enable automatic syncing. New free users will instead need to manually export and upload their data to third-party platforms. A support forum post revealed the policy shift, with many existing users criticizing the additional cost for a feature they consider basic. An official response from Withings confirmed the change, stating that automatic sync to third-party apps is now part of the Withings+ plan. The company clarified that free users will no longer have automatic sync, requiring manual data transfers. Withings, known for premium smart health devices like the $600 Body Scan 2 scale and the $280 mid-range version, faces criticism for the policy, which some view as a way to monetize a feature previously offered for free. The company has not yet provided further comments beyond the official statement. The move has drawn attention to the broader trend of health tech companies introducing subscription fees for services once available at no cost, raising concerns among users about data accessibility and pricing strategies.

item.title: Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
item.description:

Sony has launched three new Walkman portable media players, with prices starting at $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and peaking at $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. item.title: AI Startup Wants Every Company to Assign You Your Own Personal Stalker
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
An AI startup named Outlit is promoting a system that assigns every customer a personal AI agent to monitor their activities 24/7, aiming to help businesses identify upselling opportunities, improve retention, and reacquire lost leads. Founder Josh Earle told Futurism that 'every company will soon assign an AI agent to every customer to watch their every move,' framing the technology as a logical extension of existing data-trawling practices. The company’s website claims its AI agents continuously monitor customers by analyzing internal records like call logs with company representatives, as well as external sources such as social media posts and personal life details. These data points are combined to create individual customer profiles and action plans to encourage repeat business. Earle argued that businesses 'need to know what’s going on with [their customers] — from every call that they’ve had, from every interaction, from every LinkedIn,' though the article questions the necessity and ethical implications of such invasive surveillance. Outlit asserts that customer data is secure and anonymized, but the article raises doubts about the meaning of 'anonymized' when building detailed individual profiles. Earle defended the practice as legal, stating, 'There’s nothing that we’re doing that’s illegal, so we’re within our right to be able to monitor signals.' The piece critiques the startup’s approach as an extreme example of data mining, noting that while some research suggests data mining can aid customer retention, actively monitoring social media for sales opportunities represents a 'fractional improvement' at best. The article also highlights broader concerns about techno-negativity and public distrust of surveillance technologies, suggesting that even if the future is perceived as dystopian, creators should avoid actively building systems that enable pervasive monitoring.
